https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/.text: Romania says it shot down another Russian drone in its airspace July 26 (UPI) -- Romania said Sunday it shot down a Russian drone over its territorial waters in the Black Sea, marking the the third such incident in a week and prompting the NATO member to summon Russia's ambassador. Defense Minister Radu Miruța said a Romanian Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon aircraft shot down a drone that had penetrated into Romanian airspace near the delta of the River Danube in the Black Sea. The drone was first detected by radar outside Romanian airspace before continuing without authorization to a point above Sulina, Romania, Miruta said in a statement . Five minutes later at 10:13 a.m. it was shot down over the water. "Romania's safety is not defended with slogans. Congratulations to the pilots and ground support teams!" he said. "Each such incident confirms that Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine continues to generate risks beyond Ukrainian borders." Foreign Minister Oana Toiu added that Bucharest has summoned the Russian ambassador and will weigh whether to lodge a diplomatic protest over the trio of recent incidents. An initial investigation has revealed that a drone shot down on Friday "is of the Shahed type, used by the Russian Federation in the war of aggression against Ukraine," Toiu said . "It is inadmissible and intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania's airspace, which is, at the same time, NATO airspace and European Union airspace. "Such actions are unacceptable, and we treat them with the utmost seriousness, alongside our allies," she said. Romanian President Nicușor Dan similarly congratulated the pilots who carried out the missions and criticized Moscow for its "continued violation" of Romanian airspace. Prior to Sunday's latest incident, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha urged allies to craft a "comprehensive deterrence package" against Russia over its violations of Romanian airspace, calling them "a clear demonstration of the Kremlin's complete disregard for international law, national sovereignty, and European security. "The response must match the scale of the threat," he said . "We need a comprehensive deterrence package for Ukraine and Europe: stronger sanctions, maximum pressure on Russia, and a joint effort to shield Europe's skies from Russian terror." https://www.dw.com/en/russians-snap-up-n.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5In3o According to the UN, 90% of the buildings in Mariupol were damaged or destroyed in the 2022 siege Image: Evgeny Sosnovsky Advertisement Halyna Artemova, an English teacher, lived in Mariupol for almost 40 years, at Metallurgy Avenue 87. "It's my beloved city. When I look at the photos, it brings tears to my eyes. I know every crack in the asphalt, every tree," she told DW. Her apartment block in the city on the Sea of Azov was struck by a missile during a Russian attack in March 2022. Photographer Yevhen Sosnovsky and his wife lived in the house next door, Metallurgy Avenue 85, for 20 years. "I did everything myself, all the interior renovations, and the furniture," he said. "We invested a lot in it; we planned to spend our twilight years there, living quietly." His building also caught fire during the missile attack, and residents were driven out by Russian troops. They weren't even allowed to take food or clothing with them. Photographer Yevhen Sosnovsky documented his apartment before and after the Russian attack Image: Evgeny Sosnovsky Now there's a parking lot where Sosnovsky's apartment block used to be. Next door, where Artemova once lived, stands a new building. The Russian building contractor Su-2007, which operates in the Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, cleared several buildings on Metallurgy Avenue that were destroyed in the war and constructed high-rise apartment blocks in their place. These form part of a residential complex now known as the Leningradsky Kvartal. "They're building on human bones, and fast, to eradicate the traces of their crimes," said Sosnovsky. DW is not allowed in to the Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, so cannot report directly from city. However, it is possible to get an idea of what life is like in Mariupol today by talking to people who used to live there, studying satellite images, and doing research online. Newcomers benefit from cheap mortgages Many people who have moved into the new apartments on Metallurgy Avenue communicate with each other online in neighborhood forums. From these forums, it's clear that the majority bought the apartments either to live in themselves, or to rent out. In chats, they ask how they can get furniture delivered from Russia, or which kindergarten or school they should choose for their children. People are reminded that the most important thing when submitting documents is that they should be of Russian origin. Russian building contractor Su-2007 has advertised its new project in Mariupol online Image: жк-ленинградский-квартал.рф Not everyone has finished remodeling their apartments, and some people with small children take the opportunity to complain: "It's too late! Stop the goddamn renovations! Or maybe you're pro-Ukrainian and oppose Russian laws?" Economist Vyacheslav Shiryaev said apartments in the new buildings in Mariupol are being bought primarily by incomers: Russian security personnel, officials and people working in military logistics. "In addition, there are some who would just like to live by the sea but can't afford Crimea or Sochi," he said. In the Russian-occupied regions, people are offered cheap mortgages at an annual interest rate of 2% for the whole period of the mortgage — provided the borrower has Russian citizenship. The maximum they can borrow is 6 million rubles (around €63,000/$72,000), and they must be able to put down a deposit of at least 2%. Property prices have soared Dozens of apartment blocks are being built in Mariupol, and many are already occupied. Russian banks report that the port city in the occupied region tops the list for mortgage loans. Property prices have risen by a third in just one year, primarily because of the coastal location. You won't find a location like this in Russia, said Shiryaev. However, he pointed out that the apartments are of very bad quality. "Construction companies are cutting corners wherever they can, but still demanding exorbitant prices," he said. The Leningradsky Kvartal residential complex, 15 buildings of 12 to 15 floors each, is near the center of town and just 10 minutes' drive from the sea. One- and two-room apartments cost between 7.5 million and almost 10 million rubles (€104,000). Three-room apartments can be bought for upwards of 10 million rubles. Newcomers to the region are offered discounts of up to 12%. In the chats, people living in the complex say they have insured their mortgages "against war risks." If their building is destroyed, they won't have to pay back their loan. They will, however, lose their apartment. Nobody in the forum talks about the fact that there were other people living on the site of Leningradsky Kvartal just a few years ago. Dead and wounded in Mariupol According to the United Nations, 90% of the buildings in Mariupol were damaged or destroyed in the 2022 siege. Media outlets estimate that tens of thousands of people were killed. Former residents of Metallurgy Avenue told DW of neighbors who were killed or injured. Halyna Artemova lived in Mariupol for most of her life, before fleeing to Kyiv Image: Privat "A man and his son from the building next door were killed when they went out to fetch water," said Artemova. "In house number 89, a woman was buried beneath a concrete slab after a missile strike and died. A missile struck the first floor of house number 91, and a family was killed." Artemova herself was wounded by shrapnel, but managed to leave Mariupol with her elderly mother and her son. Sosnovsky was hit by a bullet. He too fled the city, with his wife and mother-in-law. Many of those who lived in buildings that were hit, but whose apartments were not destroyed, have remained in the city. However, DW was told that the occupying authorities demanded they leave their apartments nonetheless. They were promised new apartments in exchange. Ukrainian POW returns to front line after Russia torture To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video But a source told DW that none of the inhabitants of the former blocks on Metallurgy Avenue was allocated an apartment in the new Leningradsky Kvartal buildings. And those who had lost everything in the attacks could not afford a mortgage. Another source told DW that people were put in accommodation on the outskirts of town, or else in hostels. 'We were robbed of our good life' The majority of those who fled do understand why their former neighbors stayed in the city. Not everyone had the possibility of leaving Mariupol and starting again elsewhere. "The local population is being pushed out of Mariupol," said Artemova, who now lives in Kyiv with her son. Like others DW spoke with who had left the city, she said Mariupol had started to develop rapidly a few years before the Russian invasion in early 2022. People wanted to live there. "We were robbed of our ordinary life, which may have been uninteresting for some, but it was a good life. We'd go to market, knew where to buy what; we'd have a coffee, bump into a school friend with her dog and say hello," she remembered. Thousands are widely believed to have died in Russia's siege on Mariupol in 2022 Image: Evgeny Sosnovsky Neither Artemova nor Sosnovsky are considering returning to their hometown and re-registering their apartments according to the regulations of the Russian occupying authority . It's not even clear whether or not they would be allowed to enter the zone. But Ukraine is not compensating people for the loss of property there, as its authorities can't assess the situation without access to the occupied region. "They're building their shiny new houses on what used to be a graveyard. I'd like nothing better than to bomb them, but only when no one's in the buildings. It's enough to drive you to despair," said one former resident of Metallurgy Avenue. He too lived there for decades, and remembers his child's first steps, taken in an apartment that no longer exists. This is how he describes the city today: "In the center it's still OK, but if you go just a little to the left or right it smells of death." This article was originally written in Russian. Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen A company the RNLI uses for customer relations was targeted, the charity revealed. Photograph: Geoffrey Swaine/Shutterstock RNLI RNLI warns supporters their personal information may have been hacked Data raid comes amid targeting of lifeboat charity by far-right agitators who object to migrant boat rescues Haroon Siddique Legal affairs correspondent Sun 20 Sep 2026 08.28 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 11.09 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Supporters of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution have been warned that their personal information may have been stolen by hackers amid targeting of the charity by far-right agitators. In a letter accompanying the autumn copy of its Lifeboat magazine, the charity warned members that their “name, contact details and records of interactions with the RNLI” could have been breached in the raid on a company it uses for customer relationship management. The Telegraph, which first reported the story , said the RNLI told its supporters that Beacon CRM advised the RNLI to “assume that data held within its systems was taken” in a cyber-attack that affected about 1,500 charities in late July. The letter added there was no evidence to date that there had been misuse, sharing or publication of members’ personal data. But news of the breach comes after targeting of the RNLI by people who object to the charity going to the aid of people trying to reach the UK on small boats. On Thursday, it emerged that a lifeboat station in Portsmouth, close to where far-right activists tried to stop asylum seekers landing, had been forced to temporarily shut . On Sunday 6 September, activists tried to blockade the road leading to a landing spot where two RNLI crews helped bring a dinghy carrying 120 asylum seekers to Eastney in Portsmouth, a few hundred metres from the lifeboat station. Police officers were injured in clashes. In the days after, lifeboat crew members were called traitors and protests took place against the charity, including at the RNLI headquarters in nearby Poole, where a museum telling the story of the RNLI closed temporarily . Portsmouth lifeboat station took down its Facebook page and RNLI volunteers across the UK were told that they should consider not wearing the charity’s branded clothing if they felt it could put them at risk. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion RNLI steps up security after abuse by far-right agitators over small boat rescues Read more The RNLI vice-president, Sir Robin Knox-Johnston, condemned the intimidation aimed at staff and volunteers, including “online and physical abuse”, as “frankly quite disgraceful”. Far-right protesters had called for people to stop donating to the charity, but it reported that it had subsequently experienced a “significant” boost to its fundraising. It has stressed that only 1.2% of its rescue work last year – 109 callouts out of 9,058 – was to small boats in the Channel. A report on the hack published by Beacon CRM earlier this month said there was no evidence that it was a targeted attack on Beacon or any specific customer, and that the cyber-attacker had contacted it “only to indicate they would be deleting any data they have exfiltrated and no copy would be retained, sold or shared”. A spokesperson for the RNLI said: “Beacon CRM works with many charities and organisations across the UK and Ireland, and while they cannot confirm exactly which records were accessed or downloaded, it advised all affected organisations, including the RNLI, to assume that data held within its systems was taken. “At this stage, there is no evidence that information relating to RNLI supporters has been published, shared online or otherwise misused.” Explore more on these topics RNLI Cybercrime Hacking Charities Immigration and asylum Migration news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqp8.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The internet was cut in Tigray during the two-year civil war which ended in 2022 (file photo) By Kaleb Moges ,Â BBC Africa Â and Â Ondiro Oganga Published 25 September 2026, 13:34 BST Updated 3 hours ago Internet and call services have been disrupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray following the outbreak of fighting this week between regional forces and the national army. Services provided by state-owned telecoms operator Ethio Telecom have been completely cut, although those from the smaller private firm Safaricom remain operational. Internet monitoring group NetBlocks earlier posted on X that network data indicated a sub-national internet shutdown in northern Tigray. "Last night telecommunications got knocked out," Duke Burbridge, an American humanitarian worker in Tigray's capital, Mekelle, told the BBC's Newsday programme. The BBC has contacted Ethiopia's authorities for comment. Sources have told the Reuters news agency that the group which controls Tigray, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), ordered the communications blackout, with one suggesting it was to disrupt government drones. The TPLF has not commented. The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and surrounding areas. Even before the current disruption, finding video and images to establish what is happening on the ground has been a challenge. So far, other than footage from Mekelle, most of what has been shared online has been from outside the region. The young women who fought in Ethiopia's last civil war and don't want to see another one Published 6 March Burbridge said there had been a scarcity of cash in Tigray for the past eight months, with people unable to access ATMs so the lack of internet services would be "devastating for everybody". Many people rely on banking and mobile money applications for transactions, with the majority using Ethio Telecom and Safaricom's networks to access these services. On Thursday a Mekelle resident who we are only identifying as Fitsum made a similar point. He told the BBC "there is almost no cash" in the city. With the outbreak of war, people were limiting their movements and the city was all quiet - "it's like a curfew has been placed," he said. Figure caption, Tigray capital 'out of cash' as fighting escalates Clashes between Tigrayan forces and their allies and Ethiopia's federal troops broke out on Wednesday, prompting fears of a return to a full scale civil war and reports of panic buying. A humanitarian source in the neighbouring region of Afar told the AFP news agency there was "heavy fighting overnight", including drone strikes, around the town of Abala in the mountains between Afar and Tigray, as "federal forces pushed the rebels from entering the town". There have also been reports of fighting near the town of Lalibela in the Amhara region, which is home to churches hewn out of rock, recognised as a UN World Heritage site. The US has warned against travel to all three regions. During the two-year conflict which ended in 2022, Tigray was totally cut off from the outside world. Limited access to cash, food and medicine pushed hundreds of thousands into famine-like conditions. It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - with estimates that some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Sunday, the TPLF announced an alliance with six other armed groups to oust the government. On Wednesday, its forces seized control of three airports from federal police. Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray. Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/Reuters View image in fullscreen Actor Selma Blair attends Variety’s 2026 Power of Women: Los Angeles event in Beverly Hills, California, on 23 September. Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/Reuters Selma Blair Selma Blair arrested at JFK after she allegedly attacked flight attendants Several news outlets reported Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open plane door Maya Yang in New York Mon 12 Oct 2026 16.03 EDT Last modified on Mon 12 Oct 2026 18.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The actor Selma Blair was arrested on Sunday at John F Kennedy (JFK) airport in New York on allegations that she attacked flight attendants on a Delta Air Lines flight, according to officials. Blair’s arrest happened at about 11pm, after Port Authority of New York and New Jersey officials said they responded to a call “about a physically abusive passenger aboard Delta Air Lines flight 938 which was parked at the gate” at JFK after arriving from Los Angeles (LAX). Blair, 54, “was taken into custody and transported to the hospital for evaluation”, the port authority also said on Monday. “Two flight attendants also reported injuries, and one was transported to the hospital for further evaluation.” The port authority said the FBI – which handles reports of crimes on airplanes – was investigating Sunday’s allegations against Blair. Asked to comment on Blair’s arrest, a Delta spokesperson said the airline “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first”. The spokesperson added that Blair’s arrest did not affect the flight she and her fellow passengers were on – and that it still landed ahead of schedule at JFK. Several news outlets on Monday reported that Blair allegedly punched a flight attendant, bit another and tried to open the airplane door. Statements released by officials did not immediately address those reported details. But an air traffic control audio recording from the flight Blair was on captured the pilot saying “one flight attendant and one passenger … sustained some minor injuries – a bloody nose as well as some bite marks”. “I don’t think we need an ambulance or anything like that – but we just want to get some medical personnel at the gate to look at their injuries,” the pilot said, according to the recording, a copy of which was published by NBC Los Angeles. The flight controller replied that paramedics were approaching the gate – and that law enforcement was already there. The Guardian has reached out to Blair’s representatives for additional comment. Her publicist told the Hollywood Reporter: “Selma experienced a medical emergency that led to the alleged conduct. Upon landing, she received immediate medical attention and is [now] in stable condition.” Sunday marked at least the second time Blair was reported to be involved in such an incident. In 2016, she reportedly began screaming uncontrollably before being removed on a stretcher while on a Los Angeles-bound flight from Cancún, Mexico. Blair apologized after the earlier episode, saying that she “mixed alcohol with medication”. “That caused me to black out and led me to say and do things that I deeply regret,” Blair said at the time. The actor has also made news headlines for a 2018 multiple sclerosis diagnosis . And in February 2024, she apologized for an Islamophobic comment on social media. Blair’s starring film credits include Cruel Intentions, Legally Blonde and Hellboy. She earned a best spoken world album for children nomination at the 2011 Grammy awards, for her work on Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl – The Definitive Edition.
